thread_title: Sarracenia species and hybrids, Southern Baldwin Co, AL
breadcrumb: Sarracenia species and hybrids, Southern Baldwin Co, AL

posts.body_html:
Interestingly enough, this site experienced a drastic flood earlier this year, but the plants overall seemed to have been unaffected. One minute, it'll be dry, 30 minutes to an hour later, the roads are half a foot under water! These floods are likely one means by which seeds can be dispersed from one site to another, since the seeds float on the top of water. In today's world, there are very limited number of new sites that Sarracenia can colonize since everything is pretty much developed. A drainage ditch is a Sarrcenia's best bet at starting a new population.

The deep south has some extreme weather: in the winter, I've seen reports of the temperatures dropping to 5 degrees F at night, and then a few days later, it'll be in the low 70's during the day! The temperatures will swing drastically like this during the winter and early spring, and then as soon as early summer hits, it's like you're in the tropics!

With all that in mind, it's hard to understand how these plants below seemed unscathed from the harsh and unpredictable weather they've experienced. There's a lot of genetic diversity in this field, and something that caught my eye was this dark red S. leucophylla:






Here's a mitchelliana back-crossed with S. leucophylla:



S. leucophylla "flat-top": seems like a credible cultivar name, doesn't it?



S. leucophylla var. alba:


Random yet interesting clone:

posts.body_html:
thanks KE! yeah, hopefully this wasn't my last trip...my wife and I are expecting a baby girl around March of 2015, so I'm trying to get all that nerdy/risky CP travel out of my system before I'm sent to "baby jail." My wife is very helpful and hard working, so maybe family life won't be all that restrictive, but we'll see. I'm enjoying these photos too while I can, haha:







I think these green plants are very similar to the hurricane creek white plants. You can find these green and white plants in most wild populations, but they're the exception to the rule. Hurricane creek white is different because it came from a super-white var. alba, whereas this plant likely evolved from a regular leucophylla:





Water restricts growth during the drought season, so that's why you see them thriving in this ditch:



Professional photography, yeah that's right, that shadow of a hand in the foreground...it's...ahem...ummm...art...yeah!






More white plants with L. catesbaei in bloom:


Nice dense clump:





And an overview shot of the field to end the show!

posts.body_html:
KE: anytime!

Calen: Thank you! Yeah, it's crazy, and check out how deep my nerdiness runs: Aside from my wife's unquestionable psychological compatibility with me, I married her because I was trying to make a back cross: I'm 1/2 russian, 1/2 taiwanese and she's pure mainland Chinese. Dude, it's like taking a moorei from Santa Rosa Co, FL and back crossing it with a hurricane creek white clone F from Baldwin Co, AL! It's like improving a variety, LOL Figured only you guys would understand

Speaking of Mooreis, what I didn't notice until now is check out the photo of the leucophylla (with my fingers squeezing it's "cheeks") right before that dark red lipped moorei....I bet you they're related (note the similarity in shape).

Mr. Ed-glad to inspire you! The site is on a slight angle: at the top end has a spring, and it's just one huge field. Maybe 2 meters below the surface, there's water slowly running beneath the entire field, but on the surface, the soil seemed barely moist. You can see sandy crayfish mounds on what looks like dry land on the surface, it's really bizarre!

Sunbelle-you're welcome, always a pleasure to share these sites with everyone!
